persons.name: Ebenezer Goodrich
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 March 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “GOODRICH EBENEZER”, 1833-10-22: 1 parcel of the school section — lot 1 of block 93 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $100.00 (ls0168). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: GOODRICH EBENEZER matches Ebenezer Goodrich: the forename names Ebenezer Goodrich of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Goodrich, Ebenezer” (poll_1834_045, line 214). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Goodrich' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1835 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Payne, L. W.” (poll_1835_056, line 343). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Payne' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

persons.name: John Wright
persons.note: ONE OF THE TWELVE WHO VOTED FOR INCORPORATION on 5 August 1833 (Andreas prints the poll: 'John W. Wright'), one of the twenty-eight electors five days later, a candidate who took two votes, and one of the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833 and one of its three first elders. Charles Butler met him on his first morning in Chicago in August 1833, at the funeral of a child. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds, and an advertisement in it is a peculiarly good witness: the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. It is also NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period, so it is strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835.

persons.name: John S. Wright
persons.note: A MINOR IN 1833 AND A FOUNDING MEMBER OF THE FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN JUNE OF THAT YEAR - his name is in the list of nine village citizens alongside his father's. He would have been about twenty in 1835. THE RELATIONSHIP IS THIS RECORD'S READING: Andreas lists the two Wrights separately and never says they are father and son, and 'John Wright, came in 1832, a merchant' and 'John S. Wright, then a minor ... came in 1832' arriving in the same year with the same surname and joining the same church on the same day is a strong reading and not a statement.

residents.research_note: A FATHER-AND-SON HOUSEHOLD ASSEMBLED FROM TWO SEPARATE ROSTER ENTRIES, and one of only three multi-generation households in this parcel. THE ADVERTISEMENT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE PEOPLE HERE: 'Two Buildings to Let' until 1 June 1834 documents a rental market in a town of perhaps a thousand people, and this project holds a trap about that same advertisement - it carries an engraving of a three-storey building which is a jobbing printer's stock cut and NOT a picture of anything in Chicago.
